opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the bottleneck we keep running into is that a model, once it's trained, is kind of frozen in what it knows and in how well it can check itself. If you ask it to just reflect on its own answer with nothing external, it often doesn't have new information. It can rephrase its mistake more confidently, but it can't really discover that it's wrong. Pure self-reflection has a ceiling.

Tools change that, because they bring in a signal that doesn't come from the model's own head. If it writes code, it can execute it and see the error. If it does math, it can call a calculator or a solver. If it makes a factual claim, it can search and compare. Now the model has a grounded way to notice "okay, my first attempt was wrong," and the feedback is objective, not just its own opinion of itself.

What makes that exciting for learning, and not just for getting one answer right, is that those trajectories become data. You have an attempt, external feedback, a correction, and a verified final result. That's exactly the kind of signal you want for training, and it's much richer than a single human label. You can generate it at scale, and you can filter on what was actually verified as correct. So the model generates its own improvement data, grounded by the environment.

And I think that's the path past the limit of human annotation. For a lot of things we're already at the point where models write better than the average annotator, so imitating humans only gets you so far. What gets you further is the model trying things, getting feedback from the world through tools, and reinforcing what works. That loop, act, check, correct, learn, is basically how people get better at things too. You don't improve by thinking harder in a vacuum; you improve by trying and getting feedback. Tools give models that feedback, and that's why I think it's one of the most promising directions for models that keep getting better.

r001.rationale: The response describes models discovering their own errors through tool feedback and turning attempts, corrections, and verified results into training data.

r002.rationale: It explains that tool feedback can show a first attempt was wrong, and that the attempt-to-correction trajectory becomes training data. Calling it a signal for training communicates examples for updating the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that the fundamental bottleneck for these models today is not compute, it's not even really architecture, it's the data. We've essentially consumed the internet. Pretraining on more human text gives you diminishing returns, and the next frontier is the model generating signal for itself.

Now, the obvious objection to self-improvement is: if the model is wrong, and it grades itself, it just reinforces its own mistakes. You get this echo chamber effect. That's where tools come in. A tool like a code interpreter, a search engine, a calculator, a theorem prover, gives you an external source of ground truth that the model does not control. If I write a program and I run it and it crashes, that's not the model's opinion, that's reality pushing back.

So the loop becomes: the model attempts something, it calls a tool, it observes a result that it couldn't have hallucinated, and it corrects itself. And critically, that correction trajectory is itself training data. You don't need a human to annotate it. You get a verified signal, and you get it at scale, because tool calls are cheap compared to human labels.

We saw a version of this already in Llama 2 and Llama 3 work, where you have the model generate, then verify with a tool, then keep what passes. In code and math this is quite clean because the verifier is strong. The really interesting question is how far that generalizes. For writing or reasoning about the world, the verifier is softer. But I think the direction is clear: you anchor the model to something external, you let it iterate against that, and you learn from the iterations. That's how humans learn too. We don't just think harder, we check.

r001.rationale: It describes the model attempting a task, using a tool to expose errors, correcting itself, and turning that correction trajectory into training data.

r002.rationale: It says tool results and correction trajectories provide training data, but does not clearly state that the discrepancy supplies examples used to update the model’s weights.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that a model can learn from the consequences of what it does. If it writes some code, runs it, and gets an error, it has feedback. It can revise the code and try again. That’s a much richer learning signal than simply asking the model, “Are you sure?” The tool gives it something outside its own predictions to check against.

And if you train on those interactions, you can potentially turn that feedback into better behavior. The model isn’t just learning an answer; it’s learning how to notice a mistake, investigate it, and recover. Of course, correcting something in the context of a conversation isn’t the same as updating the model. You still need a training process to make those improvements persist.

What makes this promising is that, in domains where you can verify the result, you can generate more of that experience without a human having to label every step. The challenge is making sure the feedback actually measures what you care about. But that loop—act, get feedback, correct, and learn—seems like a very powerful direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes tool feedback revealing mistakes, then says training on those interactions can teach the model to notice and recover from errors. This conveys errors from self-correction as training material.

r002.rationale: The response says a training process is needed to make improvements persist, but it does not explain that differences between expected answers and tool-verified results become examples for updating model weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that generating an answer and knowing whether it’s correct are two different problems. If you ask a model to critique itself without any new information, it can just reinforce its original mistake. But give it a tool—a code interpreter, for example—and now it can run the code, see an error, and try again. It has feedback from something outside itself.

That creates a very interesting learning loop. The model attempts a task, gets feedback, corrects its answer, and then we can train on the successful trajectory. So you’re no longer relying only on humans to write the right answer for every example. You can use interaction with an environment to produce new learning signals.

The challenge is making sure the feedback actually measures what you care about. But when you can verify success, even for a subset of tasks, you have a way for the model to learn from its own experience. That’s what makes this direction exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes tool feedback exposing mistakes, followed by correction and training on the successful trajectory as a new learning signal.

r002.rationale: It says tool feedback can support training, but does not explain discrepancies between expected and verified results as examples for updating the model’s weights.
